General information.Name: The water, energy, and land footprint of tilapia aquaculture in mexico, a comparison of the footprints of fish and meat
General information.Category: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting/112 Animal Production and Aquaculture/1125 Aquaculture
General information.Description: In the food-energy-water (FEW) nexus, livestock has a dominant place. It is generally considered as water, energy and land-intensive. Aquaculture could provide additional animal protein and contribute to meeting the food demand. However, aquaculture requires natural resources and causes freshwater pollution due to aquafeed, fertilizer, and hormone use. This study assesses the sustainability of aquaculture using the indicators water footprint (WF), energy footprint (EF) and land footprint (LF), comparing results with livestock. It uses extensive, semi-intensive and intensive Tilapia aquaculture in Mexico as a case study including broodstock, breeding, fattening, processing, and transportation phases. Tilapia production in intensive aquaculture has the largest footprints. Blue WFs are smallest in semi-intensive systems; green WFs, EFs and LFs are smallest for extensive systems. For protein, tilapia from intensive systems has the largest WF (126 l/g protein), beef (51 l/g), pork (33 l/g) and poultry (14 l/g) have smaller WFs. EFs per unit of protein or nutritional energy fall in the range of values for beef, poultry and pork. LFs of Tilapia (m²/kg) are larger than LFs of poultry but fall in the range of beef and pork. Per unit of nutritional energy EFs are similar to EFs for beef but larger than EFs of poultry and pork. From a FEW nexus perspective, it is not more sustainable to replace livestock with Tilapia. Tilapia requires more freshwater than beef, pork and poultry and pollutes larger amounts of water. For energy and land, Tilapia is not the better choice, because footprints are comparable.
General information.Tags: Food energy water nexus, Aquaculture, Tilapia, Water footprint, Energy footprint, Land footprint
General information.Technology Description: The study uses the indicators water footprint (WF), energy footprint (EF), and land footprint (LF). For the WF, the study used the WF method from the Water Footprint Assessment Manual (Hoekstra et al., 2011), considering blue, green, and grey water. For the EF and LF, the study used a chain analysis approach. The study covers five production phases: (i) broodstock, (ii) breeding, (iii) fattening, (iv) processing and (v) the transportation phase.

processDocumentation.LCI method: Footprint analysis based on the Water Footprint Assessment Manual (Hoekstra et al., 2011) and a chain analysis approach for energy and land footprints.
processDocumentation.Process type: Cradle-to-gate analysis of Tilapia fillet production, including broodstock, breeding, fattening, processing, and transportation. It excludes packaging, retailing, and consumer transportation and cooking.
processDocumentation.Modeling constants: The functional unit is one ton of Tilapia fillet. Fillet yield is 33%. Intensive system refreshment rates are assumed at an average of 250% per day. Average transportation distance is assumed to be 100 km. Aquafeed composition is based on literature values (New, 1988), with all crops assumed to be grown in Mexico and fishmeal originating from tuna waste.
processDocumentation.Data source information: Data was derived from a variety of sources including: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2010b) for meat WFs; Williams et al. (2006), De Vries and De Boer (2010), and Kramer and Moll (1995) for meat EFs; Gerbens-Leenes et al. (2002) for meat LFs; SAGARPA (2013, 2015) for Mexican aquaculture statistics; Pahlow et al. (2015) for aquafeed WFs; and Flores-Nava (2007) for system parameters.
processDocumentation.Data completeness: The study covers all major production stages from egg to processed fillet. It explicitly excludes packaging, retailing, and consumer use phases.
processDocumentation.Data selection: The study focuses on inputs and outputs relevant to calculating water, energy, and land footprints. This includes direct water and energy use, as well as indirect resource use associated with aquafeed production.
processDocumentation.Data treatment: A seven-step calculation process was used: 1. Estimation of direct blue WF; 2. Calculation of direct LF; 3. Calculation of aquafeed offered; 4. Allocation of aquafeed; 5. Estimation of the WF from aquafeed; 6. Calculation of EF; and finally, 7. Calculation of the direct grey WF.
processDocumentation.Sampling procedure: Data is not based on direct sampling but on a combination of literature review, government statistics, and common practices informed by fieldwork experience.
processDocumentation.Data collection period: The article was published in 2021, using data from various sources published between 1988 and 2018.
processDocumentation.Use advice: Results are subject to uncertainty, particularly regarding water refreshment rates in intensive systems (which can vary from 100-400%), transportation distances, and specific aquafeed composition, which can significantly influence the final footprint values.
processDocumentation.Completeness: High within the defined system boundaries (cradle-to-processing), but with acknowledged uncertainties and exclusions (packaging, retail, consumer use).

processDocumentation.Intended application: To assess the water footprint (WF), energy footprint (EF), and land footprint (LF) of Tilapia produced in extensive, semi-intensive, and intensive aquacultural systems in Mexico and to compare results with footprints of different meat types (beef, poultry, pork) to inform sustainable food production and consumption within the FEW nexus.
